ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Ethyl carbamate (EC), widely found in alcoholic beverages, has been revealed to be a probable carcinogen in humans. Urethanase (EC 3.5.1.75) is an effective enzyme for the degradation of EC; however, the previously identified urethanases exhibited insufficient acid and alcohol resistance. In this study, an enantioselective amidase (AmdA) screened from Agrobacterium tumefaciens d3 exhibited urethanase activity with excellent alcohol resistance. AmdA was first overexpressed in Escherichia coli; however, the recombinant protein was primarily located in inclusion bodies, and thus, co-expression of molecular chaperones was used. The activity of AmdA increased 3.1 fold to 307 U/L, and the specific activity of urethanase with C-terminal His-tags reached 0.62 U/mg after purification through a Ni–NTA column. Subsequently, the enzymatic properties and kinetic constants of AmdA were investigated. The optimum temperature for AmdA was 55 °C, it showed the highest activity at pH 7.5, and the K m was 0.964 mM. Moreover, after 1 h of heat treatment at 37 °C in a 5–20% (v/v) ethanol solution, the residual urethanase activity was higher than 91%, considerably more than that reported thus far.

ce:sections.ce:para: Ethyl carbamate (EC) has been classified as a group 2A carcinogen, “probably carcinogenic to humans,” by the World Health Organization's International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) in 2007 (1). At present, the EC content is reduced mainly through the modification of raw materials, optimization of the fermentation process, regulation of the levels of EC precursors in fermented wine, and addition of acid urease. However, there are still many EC precursors in wines, such as urea, citrulline, arginine, hydrocyanic acid, and diethyl carbonate (2–4). Moreover, the above methods cannot eliminate the already formed EC. Therefore, using urethanase is the most direct and effective way to degrade EC.

EC can be catalyzed to ethanol, CO2, and NH3 by urethanase (EC 3.5.1.75). Urethanase can be obtained from different species of microorganisms, such as bacteria, yeast, and filamentous fungi. The urethanase from Citrobacter sp. was the first one reported (5). This kind of urethanase showed an optimal pH of 6 with a specific activity of 0.254 U/mg and a K m of 1.6 mM for EC. The enzyme retained 8.9% of its residual activity in 20% ethanol. Urethanase has also been discovered from Bacillus licheniformis IFO12107 (6); it is a 160 kDa tetrameric protein and it can maintain 64% of its enzyme activity in 20% ethanol (7). The urethanase isolated from Micrococcus sp. also showed 82% urethanase activity in 20% ethanol (8). Rhodococcus equi TB-60 urethanase, which is the first recorded sequence of urethanase (GenBank: DD291329), revealed weak activity toward EC (9). Subsequently, urethanases were isolated from several fungi. The urethanase found in Penicillium variabile JN-A525 retained 65% urethanase activity in 15% ethanol, with a K m of 27.5 mM (10,11). Lysinibacillus fusiformis isolated from the gastrointestinal tracts of mice also showed urethanase activity with a K m of 37.2 mM, but it is almost completely inactivated in a 20% ethanol solution; the accession number of the DNA sequence is KU353448.1 (12,13). Overall, these types of urethanases do not maintain their activity in alcohol solutions under acidic conditions such as in Chinese rice wine (14). Recently, an urethanase isolated from the yeast Candida parapsilosis (GenBank: BBP47208) showed high alcohol resistance, with an optimal pH of 10; it can maintain 73% activity in 20% ethanol (15). The three known sequences of urethanases all have conserved amino acid sequences of the amidase family. This indicates that amidases may be enzymatic candidates for the effective degradation of EC. Masaki et al. (16) found that the Aspergillus oryzae acetamidase can catalyze EC degradation as well. Based on these findings, we screened for a suitable amidase to degrade EC.

The Escherichia coli expression system is commonly used for the production of heterologous gene products, especially various enzymes, including urethanases. When E. coli is used as an expression host, there often exist inclusion bodies. Usually, expression reduction, tag fusion expression strategies, and molecular chaperone strategies are used to improve soluble expression (17). The co-expression of molecular chaperones is mainly used to increase protein expression in the cell and improve the folding ability of intracellular proteins, thereby increasing the expression of soluble proteins (18). The molecular chaperone protein Tf can shield the exposed hydrophobic fragments of the nascent polypeptide chain to prevent unfavorable intramolecular or intermolecular interactions in the nascent chain (19). The molecular chaperone protein DnaK-DnaJ-GrpE mainly protects the nascent polypeptide chain from abnormal interactions or error aggregation (20). The protein GroES-GroEL assists the partially folded state in overcoming kinetic obstacles and transforming into the natural state, which also has a certain protective effect on the hydrophobic area (21). The co-expression of molecular chaperones significantly improves protein solubility. For example, when SPase was co-expressed with GroES-GroEL, DnaK-DnaJ-GrpE, or GroES-GroEL-Tig, it resulted in an approximately 9-fold-greater enzyme yield (22).

In this study, we successfully selected an amidase (AmdA) from Agrobacterium tumefaciens, among seven amidases, which can efficiently catalyze the degradation of EC, and expressed it in E. coli BL21(DE3). The co-expression of AmdA and molecular chaperone teams pGro7 (GroES-GroEL), pG-TF2 (GroES-GroEL-Tig), pG-KJE8 (DnaK-DnaJ-GrpE and GroES-GroEL), pKJE7 (DnaK-DnaJ-GrpE), and pTF16 (Tf) was also investigated in an attempt to enhance the soluble expression of AmdA.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Bacterial strains, plasmids, enzymes, and chemical reagents
ce:section.ce:para: The amidase genes of A. tumefaciens d3 (AAK28498.1), Rhodococcus erythropolis CCM2595 (AGT90042.1), Sporosarcina ureae strain P17a (ARF18137.1), R. erythropolis MP50 (AY026386), Klebsiella oxytoca 1686 (CP003218.1), Burkholderia phytofirmans DSM17436 (ACD16728.1), and Microbacterium hydrocarbonoxydans (GU116480) were obtained from Tsingke Biological Technology (Beijing, China). The chaperone teams pGro7, pG-TF2, pG-KJE8, pKJE7, and pTF16 were purchased from Takara Bio (Shiga, Japan). BL21(DE3) and plasmid pET-30a (+) were obtained from the laboratory collection. All other reagents were of analytical grade or chromatographic grade and were purchased from standard suppliers.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Expression of amidase in E. coli
ce:section.ce:para: E. coli BL21(DE3) harboring the pET-30a (+)/amidase was incubated in 50 mL LB liquid medium containing kanamycin (Kan) (50 μg/mL) on a shaker at 37 °C. When the OD600 reached 0.6–0.8, isopropyl β-d-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG) was added at a final concentration of 0.5 mM, and protein expression was induced at 18 °C for 18 h.

Urethanase activity was determined using the Berthelot reaction (5) method by measuring the amount of NH3 produced from EC. The NH3 is converted to NH4 + in acid solution, and the NH4 + reacts with phenol and sodium hypochlorite under sodium nitroferricyanide catalysis to form blue-green indophenol. The absorbance of indophenol was measured spectrophotometrically at 625 nm. One unit (U) of the enzyme was defined as the amount that catalyzes the hydrolysis of EC to form 1 μmol ammonium per min at 37 °C.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Co-expression of AmdA and molecular chaperones
ce:section.ce:para: E. coli BL21(DE3)-pET-30a (+)/AmdA recombinant bacteria were optimized into competent cells. Five molecular chaperone protein plasmids (pGro7, pG-TF2, pG-KJE8, pKJE7, pTF16) were transformed into E. coli BL21(DE3)-pET-30a (+)/AmdA competent cells; these strains were named sequentially as pGro7, pG-TF2, pG-KJE8, pKJE7, and pTF16. The cells were inoculated on double antibiotic LB solid medium (containing 50 μg/mL Kan and 20 μg/mL chloramphenicol (Cm)), and the successful transformation was verified via colony PCR. The verified colonies were transferred into 5 mL LB liquid medium (containing 50 μg/mL Kan and 20 μg/mL Cm), and then to 50 mL LB liquid medium after being cultured overnight, and then incubated at 37 °C at 200 rpm, until the OD600 reached 0.6–0.8. Subsequently, 50 μL of 0.5 M IPTG inducer and 50 μL of molecular chaperone corresponding inducer (0.5 g/mL l-arabinose or 5 mg/mL tetracycline) were added, and the resulting mixture was incubated for 18 h at 18 °C, 200 rpm.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Purification of recombinant urethanase and SDS-PAGE analysis
ce:section.ce:para: The cultured bacterial solution was resuspended in phosphate buffer and ultrasonically disrupted (400 W, working for 3 s, interval 7 s). The cytolytic liquid was centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 30 min and was then passed through a Ni–NTA column. Because of the His-tag, the target protein was adsorbed on the Ni–NTA column. After elution, the eluate was ultrafiltered to obtain the target protein. The purified protein sample was subjected to SDS-PAGE on a 12% (w/v) polyacrylamide gel with a 5% (w/v) stacking gel. After electrophoresis, the gel was stained with Coomassie Brilliant Blue G250. After purification, EC was used as the enzyme substrate, and the reaction rate at different substrate concentrations (1–50 mmol/L EC) was measured. According to the relationship between the substrate concentration and the reaction speed, the kinetic parameters K m and V max were determined using the Lineweaver–Burk double reciprocal method.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Determination of the optimal pH and temperature, pH stability and thermal stability of AmdA
ce:section.ce:para: Purified AmdA was used to determine the enzyme's optimal pH, optimal reaction temperature, thermal stability, and pH stability. The enzyme reaction solution was incubated with 1% (w/v) EC under the corresponding conditions for 15 min, to test the optimal pH for AmdA activity: 0.1 M citric acid–0.2 M Na2HPO4 (pH 4 to 8), 0.07 M KH2PO4–0.07 M Na2HPO4 (pH 8 to 9), and 0.1 M glycine–0.1 M NaOH (pH 9 to 11). We chose pH 5, pH 6, and pH 8 to measure the pH stability of AmdA at 37 °C. Afterwards, under optimal pH conditions, urethanase activity was measured at 20–75 °C to determine the optimal reaction temperature and to measure the thermal stability of the AmdA.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effect of ethanol concentrations, NaCl concentrations, metal ions, and EDTA on AmdA activity and substrate specificity
ce:section.ce:para: AmdA was added to different concentrations of ethanol (0%–45%) and NaCl solutions (0%–20%). After 1 h of heat treatment at 37 °C, urethanase activity in 0.1 M citric acid–0.2 M Na2HPO4 buffer (pH 7.5) was measured at 37 °C.

Various metal ions (Cr(NO3)3·9H2O, CaCl2, Co(NO3)2·6H2O, MnCl2·4H2O, FeSO4·7H2O, CuCl2·2H2O, Al(NO3)3·9H2O, NiSO4·6H2O, ZnSO4·7H2O, MgSO4·7H2O) and EDTA were added to ddH2O at a final concentration of 1 mM, and after 10 min of heat treatment at 37 °C, urethanase activity was measured. Urethanase activity in ddH2O was also measured as a control.

Under optimal reaction conditions, the activity of the pure enzyme was measured with 1% EC, methyl carbamate, butyl carbamate, acetamide, urea, l-glutamine, and benzamide as the substrate. Considering the enzyme activity of the enzyme solution to EC as 100%, the degradation activity of the enzyme solution on different substrates was determined.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Active site analysis and homology modeling of AmdA
ce:section.ce:para: Homology modeling of AmdA was carried out using SWISS-MODEL (https://swissmodel.expasy.org/repository/). All molecular structures were visualized using the PyMOL software (https://pymol.org/2/). We used the whole plasmid PCR was used to make point mutations in the possible catalytic triad. The primers are shown as below (the underlined sites indicate mutations), K98A-F: 5′-ATCGCAGACGTCGTCTGCGTCGC-3′, K98A-R: 5′-ACGTCTGCGATGGCTATGCGA-3'; S173A-F: 5′-GCGCAGCATCGAACGGCTCG-3′, S173A-R: 5′-TCGATGCTGCGCCGGGGTT-3'; S197A-F: 5′-GGCGGCGCAATCCGGCTA-3′, S197A-R: 5′-GATTGCGCCGCCCTGG-3'.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Expression of amidase in E. coli
ce:section.ce:para: Amidases from seven different bacterial species were expressed in E. coli, and the bacterial cultures were resuspended and ultrasonically broken in phosphate buffer. E. coli expressing amidase from A. tumefaciens d3, R. erythropolis MP50, K. oxytoca 1686, M. hydrocarbonoxydans, S. ureae strain P17a, B. phytofirmans DSM17436 and R. erythropolis CCM2595, named strains A–G, respectively, were characterized for their degradation of EC in pH 4, pH 5, and pH 7 buffers. The amidase from A. tumefaciens d3 (AmdA) exhibited the highest EC degradation activity at pH 7 (97.56 U/L), with little change in urethanase activity at pH 4 (73.14 U/L). Although the amidase from R. erythropolis MP50 had the highest urethanase activity overall at pH 5 (102.44 U/L), the activity (42.69 U/L) at pH 4 was considerably lower. The other five amidases exhibited lower enzymatic activity at all pH values compared with that of A. tumefaciens d3 (Fig. 1 ). Considering that the pH value of most alcoholic beverages is around 4 and the pH stability of the amidases, we chose AmdA from A. tumefaciens d3 as the target urethanase. After purification, AmdA exhibited a specific urethanase activity of 0.62 U/mg (Table S1). The purified AmdA was analyzed via SDS-PAGE (Fig. S2), and its molecular mass was estimated to be 60 kDa, which is consistent with the predicted protein sequence molecular mass calculated to be 55.9 kDa. With EC as the substrate, the V max and K m of the purified AmdA were 0.887 μmol·mg−1min−1 and 0.964 mM, respectively.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Co-expression of AmdA and chaperones of pGro7, pG-TF2, pG-KJE8, pKJE7 and pTF16
ce:section.ce:para: By introducing additional inducible plasmids into the starting strain BL21(DE3)-pET-30a (+)/AmdA, the following molecular chaperone proteins were expressed: pGro7 (GroES-GroEL), pG-TF2 (GroES-GroEL-Tig), pG-KJE8 (DnaK-DnaJ-GrpE and GroES-GroEL), pKJE7 (DnaK-DnaJ-GrpE), and pTF16 (Tf). As shown in Fig. S1, under the same cell concentration (OD600), we obtained the highest urethanase activity when the GroES-GroEL system was co-expressed with AmdA. Compared with the original strain, urethanase activity was increased by approximately 3.1 times, reaching 307 U/L, while the urethanase activity of the other strains was lower than that of the original strain. The results of protein electrophoresis showed that all chaperone proteins were expressed normally. Compared with the starting strain, the soluble part of AmdA of strain pGro7 was significantly increased; on the other hand, the AmdA expression in the other strains was reduced considerably, and the inclusion body problem of AmdA expression has not been improved (Fig. S2).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effects of pH and temperature on urethanase activity
ce:section.ce:para: Different pH buffer systems were chosen to determine the optimal pH for the purified AmdA. The optimal reaction system for AmdA was 0.1 M citric acid–0.2 M disodium hydrogen phosphate buffer at pH 7.5. Within the pH range of 6.5–8.5, the amidase exhibited relatively high urethanase activity, being greater than 70%. When the pH was lower than 5.5, the urethanase activity decreased rapidly (Fig. 2 A). We choose pH 5, pH 6, and pH 8 to measure the pH stability of AmdA. It can be seen from Fig. 2B that AmdA has excellent pH stability between pH 6 and pH 8. In a buffer of pH 6, 37 °C for 15 h, the residual urethanase activity is greater than 90%. After 15 h in the pH 8 buffer solution, the residual urethanase activity was greater than 80%, but after 5 h in the pH 5 buffer solution, the residual urethanase activity was only 48%. Therefore, AmdA is suitable for alcoholic beverages with a neutral to weakly alkaline such as Chinese weak alkaline health-care wine (23).

When urethanase activity was measured at 20 °C–75 °C, it reached its highest activity at 55 °C, and the urethanase activity remained above 75% between 45 °C and 65 °C (Fig. 3 A). When AmdA was placed at 40 °C and 45 °C for 6 h, the urethanase activity remained above 90% and 80%, respectively. When the temperature was higher than 55 °C, the urethanase activity began to decrease. After being kept in a 60 °C water bath for 5 h, the remaining urethanase activity was less than 50% (Fig. 3B).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effects of ethanol concentration, NaCl concentration, metal ions, and EDTA on urethanase activity and substrate specificity
ce:section.ce:para: Purified AmdA was incubated in different concentrations of NaCl or ethanol buffer for 1 h (control group under the same conditions), and urethanase activity was measured. The enzyme showed excellent tolerance to low concentrations of ethanol. In 0%–20% ethanol, the urethanase activity was more than 90% that of the control, but it dropped rapidly when the concentration of ethanol exceeded 25% (Fig. 4 A). However, the enzyme exhibited poor salt tolerance. When the NaCl concentration was 5% (w/v), urethanase activity was 57% of the control activity. As the salt concentration increased, the enzyme was rapidly inactivated (Fig. 4B).

Most metal ions (at 1 mM) affected the activity of AmdA (Fig. 4C). Among them, Ca2+, Mg2+, and Co3+ can increased the activity of AmdA to a certain extent, increasing the enzymatic activities by 72.7%, 98.8%, and 18.4%, respectively, relative to the control with no metal ion. Al3+, Zn2+, and Cu2+ had strong inhibitory effects on AmdA, reducing the activity by 71.5%, 57%, and 80.3%, respectively. EDTA had almost no impact on AmdA activity, which indicates that EC degradation by AmdA does not require metal ions as prosthetic groups (15). In terms of substrate specificity, the enzyme had the highest activity with methyl carbamate as the substrate; the activity was 18% higher than that with EC as substrate (Fig. 4D). Although the previously reported urethanases were basically inactive on urea (15), AmdA in this study was 49% active on urea, but inactive on benzamide and l-glutamine.

Although AmdA exhibited a high urethanase activity under relatively high alcohol concentrations, there is currently no available 3D structure of this protein. This is an obstacle to the in-depth study of the structure and function of the enzyme. To identify and understand the function of the structural motifs of AmdA, we used the 3a1K.1. A protein, which has a 41% sequence similarity in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) with the modeling template. Through sequence analysis and structural alignment with the template, the catalytic triad was determined to be Lys 98, Ser 173, and Ser 197 (Fig. 5 A). By conserved sequence staining of the protein, it can be seen that the AmdA sequence is highly conserved near the catalytic active site (Fig. S3). To verify the accuracy of the model, each residue of the catalytic triad was mutated to Ala. The results showed that substituting Ala for the catalytic residues significantly decreased the catalytic activity, and almost inactivated the enzyme (Fig. 5B). The results were the same as the predicted model, and these three amino acids were concluded to likely be the catalytically active sites.

Urethanases from the following microbial species have been reported: Citrobacter sp. (5), R. equi strain TB-60 (9), Bacillus licheniformis IFO12107 (6), Micrococcus sp. (8), P. variabile JN-A525 (10), L. fusiformis SC02 (12,13), and C. parapsilosis (15). Only R. equi strain TB-60, L. fusiformis SC02, and C. parapsilosis have known gene sequences. Most alcoholic beverages have ethanol concentrations between 5% and 20% (v/v); when the urethanases from the above microbial species were used to degrade the EC in alcoholic beverages, relative enzyme activities ranged from 0% to 82%. In the current study, the amidase named AmdA with a known gene sequence was investigated for its high urethanase activity and excellent tolerance to relatively high concentrations of ethanol. The relative activity of AmdA was 91% in 20% (v/v) ethanol. It is known that most alcoholic beverages, especially Chinese traditional rice wines, are acidic (14). However, the Agrobacterium tumefaciens AmdA studied here is only suitable for neutral or weakly alkaline alcoholic beverages with a pH between 6 and 8. In acidic alcoholic beverages, the catalytic activity of AmdA decreases sharply, revealing its unsuitability for the degradation of EC in acidic alcoholic beverages. For AmdA to be successfully applied, it must be modified to improve its acid resistance. On the one hand, we can replace the amino acids that interact with the key amino acid residues that act as Lewis bases in the enzyme molecule, or change the charged amino acid residues on the surface of the enzyme molecule to reduce the optimal reaction pH of the enzyme reaction. On the other hand, we can use protein engineering or chemical and physical modifications in an attempt to improve the acid tolerance of AmdA and its affinity for EC.

Analysis of the amino acid sequence of AmdA revealed that it has the conserved GGSSGG sequence of the amidase signature (AS) family (24). After homology modeling, the amino acid sequences were compared, analyzed, and verified by site-directed mutagenesis. The results indicate that this enzyme belongs to the AS family, and its catalytic triad is Lys-Ser-Ser, but the mechanism of EC degradation remains unclear. However there have been several reports on the mechanism of members of the AS family, which catalyzes the hydrolysis of an amide, leading to the formation of a carboxylic acids and ammonia (25) as shown in the schematic diagram in Fig. 5C. Briefly, the active site residue Ser 173 attracts the hydrogen atom of the Ser 197 residue, and a stable hydrogen bond is formed between Ser173 and Lys 98. Then, the Ser197 residue is activated and nucleophilically attacks the carbonyl carbon atom of the substrate, inducing the substrate to form a tetrahedral transition state (26). After that, the amide bond is broken, and the ester group is connected to the Ser197 hydroxyl group through an ester bond, to forming an ester–enzyme complex (27). After the Ser173 residue transfers a proton from the hydroxyl group to the amino group, it captures the a proton from the water entering the catalyst interior (28). The resulting OH− attacks the carbonyl carbon atom of the substrate, which is attached to Ser 197, leading to the formation of another tetrahedral transition state, while Ser173 transfers the protons obtained from the water molecule to Ser-O-, and releases free ethyl hydrogen carbonate. We deduced that the mechanism may result in the formation of ammonia and ethyl hydrogen carbonate after the amide bond in EC is broken. Ethyl hydrogen carbonate is unstable in aqueous solutions, and is likely then decomposed into ethanol and carbon dioxide. However, more precise experiments and sophisticated instruments are required to prove this speculated mechanism.

Through the analysis of known urethanase gene sequences, we found that they are quite different, but have conserved GGSSGG sequences (Fig. S4). This provides a new method for the screening of urethanases that can efficiently degrade EC under high ethanol concentrations and relatively low pH conditions.
